title: Tense choice in reporting
subtitle: She said she didn't want anything to eat.
summary: Choose the tense in both the reporting clause and the reported clause according to whether the situation is finished, still true, or possibly untrue.

lesson.heading: Past situations in the reported clause
lesson.text: When the situation in the reported clause is in the past at the moment we report it, we use a past tense. If it was **already past** when it was originally spoken about, we often use the past perfect.

examples.text: 'I don't want anything to eat.' -> Yusuf said that he **didn't want** anything to eat.
'I'm leaving!' -> Lamar announced that she **was leaving**.
'We have found the missing girl.' -> Police said that they **had found** the missing girl.

lesson.note: If the order of events is already clear, the past simple is enough: She reassured me that she sent out the invitations well before the wedding. (or ... had sent ...)

lesson.heading: Present tense in the reported clause
lesson.text: If the situation is permanent or habitual, or still exists when we report it, we use a **present tense** (or present perfect) - provided the reporting verb is also in a present tense. The present perfect focuses on the result, not the action.

examples.text: Dr Weir thinks that he **spends** about five minutes on a typical appointment.
US scientists claim that they **have developed** a new vaccine against malaria.
Engineers hope that they **have solved** the problems with the bridge.

lesson.heading: After a past reporting verb, either tense is possible
lesson.text: When the reporting verb is in a past tense we can still use a present tense (or present perfect) in the reported clause. Choosing the present emphasises that the situation **still exists** or is still relevant now.

examples.text: She argued that Carl **is / was** the best person for the job.
They noted that the rate of inflation **has / had** slowed down.
They reassured us that the path **is / was** perfectly safe.

lesson.heading: Present or past - is it still true?

left.label: Present tense: probably true
left.text: The present suggests we accept the situation as fact.
examples: Yasemin told me that she **has** two houses.
*= this might suggest that it is true*

right.label: Past tense: cautious
right.text: We prefer a past tense if we are not sure the report is true, or if the situation may no longer exist.
examples: Yasemin told me that she **had** two houses.
*= perhaps this is not true, or she once had two houses but doesn't now*

lesson.heading: Tense in the reporting clause
lesson.text: To report something said or thought in the past, the reporting verb is usually past. For current news and opinions a **present** tense is possible, and often preferred, to show that what was said is still true or relevant.

examples.text: Just before her wedding, she **revealed** that she had been married before.
She **says** that she'll have to close the shop unless business improves.

lesson.heading: Three cases where the present is preferred
lesson.text: We usually choose a present reporting verb to pass on information we have heard but cannot vouch for, to quote an authority, and to report what many people say.

examples.text: I **hear** you're unhappy with your job.
The law **says** that no one under the age of 16 can buy a lottery ticket.
Every teacher I've spoken to **tells** me that standards of spelling are in decline.

lesson.text: Ask one question: is the reported situation still true now? If yes, a present tense is available even after *said*; if it is finished or doubtful, keep the past.

exercises.prompt: Match each set of words with the way it was reported.

pairs.left: 'I have never been in love with Oliver.'
pairs.right: She denied that she had ever been in love with Oliver.

pairs.left: 'Well, perhaps you're right. Maybe I did treat Lara unkindly.'
pairs.right: She conceded that perhaps she had treated Lara unkindly.

pairs.left: 'I seem to remember that Wilma's great-grandmother was from Spain.'
pairs.right: She recalled that Wilma's great-grandmother was from Spain.

pairs.left: 'I think the vase is around 250 years old.'
pairs.right: She estimated that the vase was around 250 years old.

pairs.left: 'I've told you once. I've already seen the film.'
pairs.right: She repeated that she had already seen the film.

exercises.prompt: 'Markus has stolen jewellery from my house.' -> She alleged that Markus ___ jewellery from her house.
exercises.explanation: The theft was already past when she spoke, so the past perfect is natural; the past simple is also possible because the order of events is clear.

exercises.prompt: Engineers hope that they ___ the problems with the bridge now that new supports have been built.
exercises.explanation: The reporting verb is present and the result still matters now, so the present perfect fits.

exercises.prompt: ___ that you want to buy a second-hand car. Your brother just told me.
exercises.explanation: A present tense reports information we have been told but cannot confirm.

exercises.prompt: Health officials warn that anyone who ___ directly at the sun during an eclipse may put their sight at risk.
exercises.explanation: This is a permanent, general truth reported with a present reporting verb, so the reported clause stays present.

exercises.statement: When I mentioned to Nokes that he had been seen in a local shop last Monday, he protested that he is at home all day.
exercises.explanation: ... he protested that he was at home all day. The situation being reported is finished, so it needs a past tense.

exercises.statement: Nokes alleges that he is a good friend of Jamie Barnes.
exercises.explanation: Correct. The friendship still exists and the reporting verb is present, so the present tense is right.

exercises.statement: Barnes confirmed that he is in the area of the paint factory last Monday.
exercises.explanation: ... confirmed that he had been (or was) in the area of the paint factory last Monday. Last Monday is finished time.

exercises.statement: He maintains that he was a very honest person and would never be involved in anything illegal.
exercises.explanation: ... maintains that he is a very honest person ... His claim is about how he is now, so use a present tense.

exercises.prompt: You want to hint that you doubt her story. Yasemin told me that she ___ two houses.
exercises.explanation: A past tense after a past reporting verb suggests the claim may not be true, or is no longer true.

exercises.prompt: Does the reported clause need a present tense or a past tense here?
categories: Present - still true or still relevant
Past - finished, or perhaps not true

items.text: The current law states that an employee ___ the right to appeal.
Simon accepts that he still ___ a lot to learn.
Health officials warn that anyone who ___ at the sun may damage their sight.
Yusuf said that he ___ anything to eat.
Police said that they ___ the missing girl.

exercises.prompt: Report what the law says. Put the words in order.
words: no one under the age of 16
exercises.answer: The law says that no one under the age of 16 can buy a lottery ticket
exercises.explanation: A present reporting verb is preferred when we quote an authority.
